subject: Biology
title: Autoimmune Diseases
description: Learn Autoimmune Diseases in one minute.

hook.text: In autoimmune diseases, the immune system attacks the body's own healthy cells—friendly fire.

buildup.text: Type 1 diabetes occurs when immune cells destroy insulin-producing cells in the pancreas.

discovery.text: Rheumatoid arthritis attacks joints. Multiple sclerosis attacks nerve insulation. Lupus attacks many organs.

twist.text: Women are three times more likely to develop autoimmune diseases—and scientists still aren't sure why.

climax.text: Over 80 autoimmune diseases are known. Together, they affect about 5–8% of the population.

punchline.text: When the army turns on its own country.

quiz.question: What happens in an autoimmune disease?
options: The immune system attacks healthy body cells
The immune system shuts down completely
Pathogens disable all white blood cells

details.summary: Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own cells and tissues. In rheumatoid arthritis it targets joints, in type 1 diabetes it destroys insulin-producing cells, and in multiple sclerosis it attacks nerve coatings.
details.whyItMatters: Autoimmune diseases affect roughly 5 to 8 percent of the global population. Understanding how immune tolerance breaks down is crucial for developing treatments that suppress harmful self-attack without compromising defense against real infections.
takeaways: Autoimmunity results from immune cells failing to distinguish self from foreign
Over 80 autoimmune diseases target different organs and tissues
Treatments suppress immune activity but may increase infection vulnerability

faq.question: Why does the immune system turn against the body's own cells?
faq.answer: Normal immune development eliminates self-reactive cells, but some escape this screening. Triggers like infections, stress, or environmental factors may then activate these cells. Molecular mimicry, where pathogen antigens resemble self-antigens, can also initiate autoimmune attacks.

faq.question: Why are autoimmune diseases more common in women?
faq.answer: Women are affected 2 to 10 times more often than men for most autoimmune diseases. Estrogen enhances immune responses, the X chromosome carries many immune genes, and microchimerism from pregnancy may trigger self-reactivity. The exact mechanisms remain under active research.
